extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; creative writers interested in salon-era epigrams, maxims, and epistolary style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing concise, polished maxims, epigrams, and graceful epistolary prose in the French salon tradition—focusing on terseness, finish, taste, and the social role of encouragement. Useful for writers trying to emulate sententious salon-style expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terseness / Concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce generalizations to their briefest form of expression, to give them the epigrammatic turn which made them portable in the memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The salon’s specialty was to compress morals and observations into short, memorable maxims. Examples: the habit in Madame de Sablé’s circle of producing compact 'maxims' and Pascal’s Pensées being remodelled toward terseness. Anti-pattern: leaving thoughts as raw, extended 'materials' rather than shortening them into portable statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish / Polish
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring thoughts to the highest degree of terseness and finish by repeated revision and careful shaping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscripts show ideas were 'remodelled again and again' to achieve finish; one should 'cut into facets, and polished like amethysts or emeralds.' Practical guidance: revise repeatedly to pare and refine wording until maximum effect is obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epigrammatic Piquancy / Sententiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for an epigrammatic, sententious turn—wittily condensed truth or paradox that has bite and memorability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The salon prized maxims with epigrammatic piquancy (La Rochefoucauld’s Maxims are the exemplar). The social practice included inventing maxims as salon entertainment. Anti-pattern: maxims that are polished but lack genius or individual stamp (Madame de Sablé’s maxims compared unfavorably to La Rochefoucauld’s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of Good Taste and Good Sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine good taste (elegant style) with good sense (sound judgment and clarity) in epistolary and salon writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters and short pieces should be a 'happy mixture of good taste and good sense'—neither pretty affectation nor barren wit alone. Example: Madame de Sablé’s epistolary examples are praised for this balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony and Moderation (Subtlety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor harmonious blending of qualities and moderate expression rather than extreme, showy traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal effect is not produced by a single striking quality but by an 'entire being' whose blended virtues 'give repose to the eye.' Avoid 'tons criards' (shrill tones) or flashy mannerisms that weary the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightness, Ease, and Grace in Epistolary Prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for light, pretty letters 'made out of almost nothing'—effortless grace and apparent spontaneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The quoted letter illustrates a modest, indirect, ingenuous tone that conveys esteem without ostentation. Practical note: cultivate ease and an artful lightness rather than heavy apologetics or overwrought defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision as Craftsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat writing as a craft: remodel, pare, and polish lines and thoughts until they achieve facet-like clarity and brilliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly supported by the observation that Pascal’s Pensées were remodelled multiple times; the metaphor of cutting and polishing gems underscores iterative editing and attention to form and surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate Clearly Rather Than Flaunt Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize clear communication of thought over conspicuous display of originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns of writers who 'neglect... the successes of the salon' and 'the effort is not to betray originality rather than to communicate it.' In practice, avoid obfuscation or mannered novelty that obscures meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulate and Support Others (Sympathetic Criticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Serve as a sympathetic, appreciative reader or interlocutor who encourages and draws out the originality of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madame de Sablé’s chief literary role was to 'second a man’s wit with understanding'—valued as an intellectual office. Guidance for collaborative/social literary contexts: praise, sympathy, and receptivity are creative contributions in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit Form to Medium and Audience (Salon Conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose forms and stylistic conventions suited to the salon or social setting—short maxims and epigrams for salon exchange, polished essays and Pensées for wider publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage contrasts salon-bred portable maxims with longer works; stylistic choices should reflect whether one writes for conversational portability (sententious, memorable lines) or for the press/a broader public (different scale and aims).
